_what: EA-CORPORA-19 seat specification: four seats — the Pearl poet, Rumi's Masnavi, Gibran's The Prophet and Blake's illuminated books — each in its original language, public domain in the United States. Read by build_seats.py. Every locus listed here is kept only if the string is found in the seated text; the builder reports any that are not.
_ruling: Lee Sharks, 2026-10-18: "did we ever seat the medieval pearl poem in the originals library?" — "rumi, too - and gibran's the prophet if its public domain" — "and blake" — "yes, original language where available always, the prophet full, and lets do illuminated books as text to start. we can group those all in a single ea-corpora deposit, refer to examples, and they also do to alexanarch data and get spines and cards on traininglayerliterature's originals library".

seats.title: The Pearl Poet — Pearl, Cleanness and Patience (British Library, MS Cotton Nero A.x): Morris's First Edition, the Manuscript in Facsimile, and Gollancz's Pearl

license.payload: Public domain: the poems are anonymous, of the late fourteenth century. Morris's edition (Early English Text Society, 1864; second edition 1869), Gollancz's Pearl (London: David Nutt, 1891) and the EETS facsimile of the manuscript (Oxford University Press for the EETS, 1923) are public domain in the United States (published before 1931). Project Gutenberg packaging under the PG licence; Internet Archive scans of public-domain volumes.
license.record: CC-BY-4.0 applies to this seat record only.

seats.scope: Pearl, Cleanness and Patience in their first edition, with the manuscript itself in the 1923 facsimile, and Gollancz's Pearl of 1891 with its modern rendering on the facing page. Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, the fourth poem of Cotton Nero A.x, is in the facsimile and not otherwise seated in this pass: QUEUED (Morris, EETS o.s. 4, 1864, is public domain). Modern editions (Gordon 1953; Andrew and Waldron) are in copyright and are not seated. St. Erkenwald, sometimes given to the same poet, is in another manuscript and is not seated.
seats.why_seated: The poem whose name the archive's own Pearl and Other Poems (2014) carries, seated so the name has its source on the shelf. A father who has lost a pearl in the grass, his daughter, dead before she was two, falls asleep where it fell and sees her across a river in the New Jerusalem of Revelation 21: the archive's Revelation line meets it there.

seats.title: Jalal al-Din Rumi — Masnavi-yi Ma'navi, the Six Books, in Persian (Ganjoor)

license.payload: Public domain: Rumi d. 1273. The transcription is Ganjoor's (ganjoor.net), which names its source for each section and states of its texts: 'هم‌اکنون منبع عمدهٔ آثار موجود در این مجموعه منابع آزاد در دسترس همگان است' (the principal source of the works in this collection is free sources available to all), releasing them on the principle 'دگران کاشتند و ما خوردیم، ما بکاریم و دیگران بخورند' (others planted and we ate; we plant and others will eat). Ganjoor's statement is recorded as given; it is not a formal licence.
license.record: CC-BY-4.0 applies to this seat record only.

loci: masnavi-daftar-1

Book One, section 1 (سرآغاز), the first couplet: 'بشنو این نی چون شکایت می‌کند / از جدایی‌ها حکایت می‌کند' — the Song of the Reed
seats.scope: The Masnavi entire, all six books, in Persian, one text per book. Ganjoor's prose summaries of couplets and its recitations are not seated. The printed edition behind the transcription is not stated in the fetched data beyond Ganjoor's per-section source name, which is recorded. Nicholson's critical edition (Leiden: Brill, 1925–1933) and his translation are not seated: original language only, by ruling. Whinfield's abridged English (1887; 1898) is public domain and not seated for the same reason. The Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi is not seated in this pass: QUEUED.
seats.why_seated: Rumi asked for by name, in the original. The Masnavi opens with the reed cut from its bed and telling the story of its separation: transmission out of loss, the archive's oldest subject, from the other side of the medieval world.

seats.title: Kahlil Gibran — The Prophet (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1923), with the Author's Twelve Drawings

license.payload: Public domain in the United States (first published 1923; public domain since 1 January 2019) and in the EU (Gibran d. 1931). Written by Gibran in English, its original language. The later printing's front matter (the Bragdon epigraph, a list of the author's books) is recorded as it stands and adds nothing to the book's text. Project Gutenberg packaging under the PG licence.
license.record: CC-BY-4.0 applies to this seat record only.

seats.scope: The book entire, all twenty-six sermons with the coming of the ship and the farewell, and the twelve drawings. Gibran's Arabic works are not seated in this pass; The Prophet's original language is English.
seats.why_seated: Asked for in full. A book of sayings delivered by a departing teacher to a city that kept him twelve years: the farewell discourse as a genre, beside the Gospel of John the archive reads in its own seats.

The Songs (London: R. Brimley Johnson; Guildford: A. C. Curtis, 1901) and the Marriage (Boston: John W. Luce, 1906) public domain. seats.scope: The illuminated books as text, to start, by ruling: every one of them in Keynes's 1925 edition, the standard text before Erdman, with the Songs and the Marriage also as proofread texts. Keynes's three volumes carry Blake's other writings bound in with the illuminated books (Poetical Sketches, Tiriel, The French Revolution, Vala or the Four Zoas, the prose, letters and annotations); they are seated with the volumes and are not counted as illuminated. The plates as images (the Blake Archive) are not seated in this pass: QUEUED. Erdman's Complete Poetry and Prose (1965; 1982) is in copyright and is not seated.
seats.why_seated: Blake asked for by name. The prophetic books are the one English body that builds its own mythology, its own names and its own cosmos and prints them as one object, word and image together: the Hexagon's nearest precedent in the language.
